title: AESO REM: the shift to a nodal market
snippet: The Alberta Electric System Operator (AESO) is currently implementing a major transformation of its electricity market. In this article, we explore the three key changes that will most impact power trading...
fullText:
The Alberta Electric System Operator (AESO) is currently implementing a major transformation of its electricity market. In this article, we explore the three key changes that will most impact power trading companies.
          

      

AESO’s Restructured Energy Market (REM) design was published in 2025 and the associated REM ISO rules received ministerial approval in March 2026. AESO’s IT roadmap provides for a participant soft launch beginning in January 2027, system trials starting in Q3 2027, and targeted production market cutover in Q2 2028.1

The production target should not be mistaken for the deadline to begin preparing. Participants need to assess impacts, assign ownership, make platform and data decisions, and prepare for early system access and testing during 2026. 

REM aligns Alberta more closely with market practices used across major North American ISOs and RTOs, including security-constrained dispatch and locational pricing. However, REM is not a direct copy of ERCOT or any other market. AESO has developed the design around Alberta’s energy-only market, competitive-offer framework, reliability requirements and provincial policy direction.

Below we examine the three changes likely to have the most impact on power trading companies operating in the Alberta market and explore how these changes are interconnected:

    

Locational marginal pricing (LMP) 

    

Security-constrained economic dispatch (SCED)

    

Congestion exposure and risk management 

Locational marginal pricing 

Today, Alberta’s wholesale spot energy market settles at a common province-wide pool price. REM introduces locational marginal pricing (LMP), which means every location or node on the network can have its own price.  

This necessitates a shift in focus from trading simply energy to trading energy plus location. The geography of the market and the transmission map become critically important.  

Not all market participants will settle at a nodal price. Under the REM design, source assets and controllable sink assets are subject to LMP, while eligible non-controllable sink assets generally use the Alberta Load Price (ALP) unless they elect LMP. Each locational price reflects an energy component together with location-specific congestion and marginal losses.

Transmission constraints will cause locational prices to shift and diverge. Along with LMP pricing, REM will transform congestion from being an operational concern for the market operator into a trading concern – and therefore also a potential trading opportunity. 

Trading companies will need to incorporate transmission analytics into their trading strategies, including monitoring constraints, outage forecasts and flow forecasts. Congestion risk will be embedded in every nodal power position.  

Traders will need to predict which transmission constraints will bind when, and the impact that will have on the locational pricing forecasts. In the redesigned market, trading risk will be magnified because locational prices may separate when power cannot physically flow where it is needed.  

Security-constrained economic dispatch

In a power market with a single market price, traders think primarily in terms of supply and demand balance, with the marginal resource setting the market price.  

In the REM real-time market, AESO will determine dispatch and pricing through a security-constrained process that accounts for market offers, system limits and transmission constraints. The market-clearing process will normally run every five minutes. It will seek economically efficient, physically feasible dispatch by minimizing offer-based dispatch costs while respecting system constraints. Under REM, real-time energy and the 30-minute ramping reserve product (R30) will be co-optimized.  

SCED determines which generators should run and the marginal cost of serving an additional megawatt-hour (MWh) of energy at every pricing node on the grid. That marginal cost becomes the locational marginal price at every location. Therefore, LMP pricing is the byproduct of the SCED optimization problem.  

AESO’s optimization changes under REM because it includes the physical constraints of the network when determining which generation resources will run. In an SCED market, the trader must consider the optimization logic employed by the market operator and how that optimization will influence various market prices. The trader must consider transmission constraints that may lead to generators in different regions becoming the marginal resource.  

Traders will need to understand market constraints, when and where transmission congestion will appear, and how long it will last. This requires more precise forecasting of regional renewable generation, localized demand forecasts, and the anticipation of transmission congestion. 

Traders must also become aware of transmission outages and the impact those outages have on dispatch and therefore on LMP pricing. The trading risk profile becomes significantly more complex, requiring analysis of demand, generation, transmission constraints and the market’s dispatch optimization.  

Congestion exposure and risk management 

After AESO’s REM implementation, congestion will be reflected in LMP prices and traders will be exposed to congestion pricing. That exposure cannot currently be hedged through an AESO-administered financial transmission rights (FTR) market, although bilateral and forward arrangements remain relevant options.  

Following its 2026 consultation, AESO decided not to advance a centralized FTR market at this time. It is instead exploring data and reporting to support voluntary risk management and market metrics that could inform any future reconsideration.

During the initial rollout of REM, traders will be exposed to locational congestion risks without a centralized FTR market and should therefore assess contractual, portfolio and operational risk-management options.  

Transitioning from single-price to security-constrained nodal markets

To prepare for the upcoming changes in the Alberta power market, power trading companies will need to examine and enhance trading strategies, business processes and systems across several dimensions:  

    

Trade capture

    

Position management 

    

Forecasting 

    

Market analytics

    

Risk analytics 

    

Reporting

    

Settlements

    

ETRM systems 

    

Bid-to-bill systems 

    

SCADA/telemetry systems 

    

Market interfaces and integration

The transformation is not limited to forecasting or trading strategy. REM also introduces new energy-offer structures, R30 participation, five-minute dispatch and settlement intervals, and updated market-power mitigation. These changes create dependencies between market strategy, offer approvals, operator actions, interfaces, metered volumes, settlement calculations and financial controls.

The most important commercial challenges are the need to understand where power will be most valuable and when transmission constraints will cause prices to separate.  Transmission becomes an important input into trading decisions, necessitating a shift to locational price forecasting, transmission congestion forecasting, along with outage and constraint analysis. These changes introduce new dimensions to position analysis, risk management, hedging, exposure analysis and risk reporting.  

In addition to evaluating trading strategy and risk analytics capabilities, trading companies need to analyze their system landscape. SCED, LMP pricing and new market products increase the volume, frequency and complexity of market data and transactions. As a result, ETRM, bid-to-bill, SCADA/telemetry, and settlement systems will need to operate in a more closely integrated manner to effectively support the trading business.  

For example, a generator may need its bid-to-bill platform to construct and submit revised energy offers, retain dispatch instructions and operator actions, and associate metered volumes with the relevant five-minute prices. Downstream settlement and finance systems then need to reconcile expected revenue with AESO results. Inconsistent asset identifiers, timestamps, or data version can create errors that are difficult to identify after the fact.

AESO plans to provide participant access through its soft-launch window beginning in January 2027, followed by collaborative trials from Q3 2027. Market participants therefore have less time than the Q2 2028 production target might suggest to confirm requirements, configure interfaces and controls, obtain test access, and demonstrate operational readiness.

Firms should begin now with a cross-functional REM impact assessment covering trading, market operations, technology, data, settlement and compliance. They should then prioritize material gaps, assign accountable owners, secure budgets, and establish a sequenced implementation and testing roadmap rather than wait for every technical specification to be finalized.

How Capco can help 

Capco helps power trading companies prepare for market transitions through trading and risk capabilities, ETRM and bid-to-bill modernization, operating-model change, and market-systems integration. For example, Capco has supported power-market clients adapting to ERCOT’s Real-Time Co-optimization plus Batteries (RTC+B) changes, including SCADA-related capabilities and trading-system enhancements. This work has included support for battery resource commissioning, operator transitions and trading-logic implementation to address evolving market and operational requirements.

For Alberta participants, the immediate priority is to translate REM requirements into a fact-based readiness plan: identify material operating and technology gaps, design a target architecture, and sequence implementation and trial preparation. Capco can support readiness assessment, operating-model and integration design, testing, and cutover planning as participants prepare for the restructured market. 

References

1 https://www.aeso.ca/transition/it-systems/

title: T+1: from operational readiness to sustainable settlement performance
snippet: With the T+1 go-live date across the UK, EU and Switzerland now 12 months away and the first regulatory milestone arriving in December, the focus is increasingly shifting from policy design to execution and...
fullText:
With the T+1 go-live date across the UK, EU and Switzerland now 12 months away and the first regulatory milestone arriving in December, the focus is increasingly shifting from policy design to execution and operational readiness, including process automation, system upgrades, liquidity and funding arrangements and coordinated industry testing. Capco’s Rollo Burgess and Elisabeth Plakinger discuss what has changed since our last T+1 readiness conversation in March, new priorities and concerns, strategic versus tactical approaches and what should senior managers be asking of their T+1 programs.

          

When we spoke earlier this year, you highlighted a number of potential pressure points around the transition. Has anything materially changed and are firms where you’d expect them to be at this point?

Rollo Burgess: Broadly speaking, across the larger broker-dealers and custodians I work with, the short answer is yes, they are. A few things have changed, though. There are some technical elements that have come to light and increased in importance in the course of the year, for example, around the Gating Event (a new settlement convention, related to securities financing transactions), which is a big topic, potentially bigger than people were expecting.1

There have been some global changes outside of the EU, UK, Switzerland in terms of the T+1 trajectories. For example, Turkey and Hong Kong have caused some level of challenge through later announcement of plans and firms have needed to assess from a governance perspective how to address these emerging priorities around the world (e.g. ‘do I run one global program or not?’).  

One of the bigger contextual challenges is the fact that many organizations are now thinking about how to deploy AI across their businesses. That was the case in the spring, and it’s even more prominent now. While AI can assist your journey towards T+1, it does mean that the change capacity is in shorter supply. It’s a fast moving and fast changing environment with many dependencies, and management bandwidth is under stress.  

Elisabeth Plakinger: The challenge has shifted from defining requirements to demonstrating operational readiness. While the industry has established the testing windows for 2027, firms are still determining which scenarios, counterparties and market infrastructures they can realistically test. 

The priority is risk-based testing of changed functionality, critical exceptions and cross-border flows, supported by production metrics that already reveal weaknesses in allocation, confirmation, matching and settlement processes. The remaining challenge is ensuring that clients, custodians and other market participants can meet the compressed timelines. 

The question is no longer simply whether individual institutions are ready, but whether the entire settlement chain can operate within T+1 timelines. Large institutions may have mature programs, but their settlement performance still depends on clients, counterparties, custodians and market infrastructures. 

Smaller asset managers and clients relying on manual allocations and confirmations are a particular concern. Firms need to identify these dependencies through actual transaction data and targeted client engagement rather than relying solely on program-level readiness assessments.

In March, the expectation was that manual processes, exceptions and legacy ways of working were all areas likely to come under pressure. What progress are you seeing there? Are the same issues still the biggest focus? 

Elisabeth Plakinger: Manual exception handling remains a significant risk because T+1 leaves substantially less time to investigate and repair transactions. The challenge extends beyond standing settlement instructions (SSIs) to the accuracy and timeliness of settlement locations, instrument data, client information and trade allocations. 

For example, a client may populate the place of settlement (PSET) during confirmation, but that information may not match the actual settlement location. The result is a downstream matching break that still requires manual intervention. 

The priority should be eliminating recurring exceptions at source and automating time-critical processes. AI can support these improvements, but it is not a substitute for accurate data and reliable operating processes.

    

  

        

      
          

                
                
            

              It's incumbent on larger firms and the industry as a whole to support smaller and regional market participants… that’s where a lot of focus will be in 2027.
            

          

            

              – Rollo Burgess
            

          

      

  

      

External dependencies were another major theme. As firms have progressed their own programs, has readiness across clients, counterparties, custodians and vendors kept pace?

Rollo Burgess: I would say largely yes, but we won’t really know until we get further ahead. In general, across the large brokers and custodians those external dependencies should be under control and being managed effectively. It’s incumbent on those firms and the industry as a whole to support smaller market participants and regional market participants in making the T+1 transition. That's where a lot of the focus will be as we go through 2027. 

Elisabeth Plakinger: External dependencies remain one of the largest uncertainties. Firms need more than confirmation that a custodian, CSD or technology provider has a T+1 program. They need clarity on when specifications will be finalized, which functionality will be available, which test environments are connected and which scenarios can be executed across the settlement chain. 

A particular challenge is that individual infrastructures may offer testing without supporting a fully connected end-to-end market test. Firms therefore need to distinguish between dependencies that are being monitored and those for which readiness has actually been demonstrated.

With the December 2026 regulatory milestone approaching, where should firms be focusing their attention between now and then?2 And what would concern you if it was still unresolved at year-end?

Elisabeth Plakinger: The immediate priority is trade-date allocation and confirmation performance. Firms should already know which clients provide accurate and complete information on time, where manual intervention remains necessary and which counterparties consistently miss the required timelines. 

By year-end, I would expect firms to demonstrate measurable improvements in these areas, supported by targeted client outreach and remediation. Simply increasing automation is not sufficient if the underlying data remains inaccurate or arrives too late. 

Rollo Burgess: SSI handling is a key recommendation. The extent to which more market participants are integrating with the various electronic platforms and using them for the distribution and management of SSIs – other than emailing – will be a good barometer of how the whole ecosystem is modernizing. That will be an interesting test, and while we won't find out immediately at the beginning of December; it will become apparent as we go through 2027. 

 

    

  

        

      
          

                
                
            

              Managing external dependencies and ensuring market-wide readiness will be key to achieving T+1 readiness collectively.
            

          

            

              - Elisabeth Plakinger
            

          

      

  

      

As programs have moved from planning to implementation what new priorities have emerged that perhaps weren’t obvious six months ago?

Rollo Burgess: I'd call out the handling of the Gating Event as a more prominent change than people imagined earlier in the year and something the industry is trying to get right.

The other new priority we're encouraging our clients to focus on is thinking not just about achieving T+1 settlement for a high proportion of trades, but also achieving that while preserving or even improving the efficiency of their inventory management and funding processes.

There's achieving T+1 and then there's achieving it in the right way. If it is achieved at the cost of a significantly increased level of borrowing, stock borrowing and so forth in order to support your settlement processes, then that will eat into your already thin margins.

As more processes move to same-day, optimizing your inventory and funding requirements should be a key initiative. The benefit won't necessarily show up in your settlement performance number next October, but it will impact business performance if you don't get it right.

Are firms using T+1 as an opportunity to remove the root causes of exceptions and improve their operating models? Or are you seeing tactical fixes designed simply to get them over the line?

Rollo Burgess: In terms of the clients I'm working with, people are using this as an opportunity to improve their process strategically. They are making fundamental changes in their technology infrastructure and moving to a different and compressed workflow. I certainly don't think that firms are approaching this purely tactically.

Having said that, I do think there will inevitably be some tactical fixes and last-minute scrambling to get over the line. The challenge for everyone is to minimize this and ensure that, wherever it does occur, it remains a temporary phenomenon.

    

  

        

      
          

                
                
            

              If you achieve T+1 at the cost of having a significantly increased level of borrowing, stock borrowing and so forth to support your settlement processes, then that will eat into your already thin margins.
            

          

            

              - Rollo Burgess
            

          

      

  

      

What are some of the practical steps Capco is taking to support our clients through the transition? What are we hearing from clients now? Where are they most confident and where are they asking for the most help?

Elisabeth Plakinger: Clients increasingly need support translating T+1 requirements into measurable operational changes. This includes analyzing existing allocation, confirmation and settlement performance, identifying recurring exceptions, prioritizing automation and assessing dependencies across clients, custodians and market infrastructures.

Testing is another important area. We help clients define a proportionate, risk-based approach that focuses on changed functionality, market-specific requirements, critical exceptions and processing capacity rather than attempting to test every existing transaction flow.

Our experience across capital markets operations, technology delivery and the US T+1 transition allows us to connect regulatory requirements with the practical changes needed to achieve sustainable settlement performance.

Rollo Burgess: There are a few practical initiatives we’re running with clients right now, such as facilitating collaboration across the ecosystem – for example, getting groups of clients together and encouraging them to collaborate and think about how they can approach the transition, working with peers across the industry.

We're doing a great deal of work on leveraging AI and AI-driven process transformation and optimization (for example using AI tooling to manage aspects of operational client interaction), which is related to firms’ T+1 programs in many cases. Our Capital Markets Smart Suite offers modular AI solutions for trusted data, operational control and scalable value across the trade lifecycle.3 This is anchored in decades of capital markets domain expertise, technical delivery capability, governance, architecture, data and change execution.

Moving to T+1 settlement touches a lot of different processes and parts of the organization. One of the most complicated aspects of delivering that in a large firm is the sheer scale of internal dependency management. Typically, T+1 isn’t the only transformation program firms are running. There is a lot of complexity in terms of how to manage and sequence the volume of change that's going through the end of this year and through next year, and that will only intensify.

    

  

        

      
          

                
                
            

              A genuinely T+1-ready firm should be able to demonstrate efficient collaboration across the market - with clients, external providers and counterparties.
            

          

            

              - Elisabeth Plakinger
            

          

      

  

      

What should senior leaders be asking of their T+1 programs for now? What evidence would convince you that an organization is genuinely on track rather than simply reporting that it is?

Rollo Burgess: They should be asking about three categories of things. Firstly, let's talk through database detail on your principal fail reasons, what's driving those fails and what you’re doing about them. They should be asking to see that data organized by client, market and other dimensions. You can tell a lot from how much insight organizations have and how focused their changes are on the root causes of fails.

Secondly, integration and engagement with inventory management and funding processes is something else I'd be asking about. Have you considered this and are you working on this in terms of how you're managing your inventory, funding, treasury implications, etc?

The final question I'd ask would be about clients. Have all our clients heard from us on this topic? Have we heard from them? What are they saying? What are their concerns? At this stage, firms should be very much in a two-way dialogue with key clients about T+1. We are seeing that as a big focus with our clients.

If we revisited in early 2027, what would you expect the genuinely T+1-ready firm to be able to demonstrate?

Elisabeth Plakinger:

 By early 2027, I would expect firms to demonstrate readiness through evidence rather than program status reports. That means measurable improvements in trade-date allocations, confirmations and matching, fewer recurring exceptions and a clear understanding of which clients and external dependencies still present risks.

They should also be able to show that critical scenarios have been tested, including gating, cross-border settlement and processing under compressed timelines. Where full end-to-end industry testing is not possible, the remaining risks need to be explicitly identified and managed.

Finally, readiness must be economically sustainable. Achieving T+1 by adding manual shifts, increasing stock borrowing or holding larger liquidity buffers may protect settlement performance in the short term, but it is not an efficient long-term operating model.

With the transition approaching, now is the time to move beyond planning and validate operational readiness across processes, technology, counterparties and exception management. Contact us to discuss how to assess your T+1 readiness, identify remaining gaps and prioritize the actions needed ahead of the December 2026 regulatory milestone and October 2027 go-live date.

References

1 The T+1 Gating Event is a new settlement mechanism that holds flagged instructions and automatically releases them at 11:00 CET on settlement day, helping synchronize settlement and preserve netting and liquidity efficiency (source: https://www.icmagroup.org/News/news-in-brief/icma-welcomes-publication-of-eu-t-1-industry-committee-guidance-on-the-gating-event)

2 7 December 2026 marks the first EU T+1 regulatory milestone, with new CSDR requirements for trade allocation and confirmation processes coming into effect ahead of the October 2027 transition (source: https://www.esma.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2026-01/EU_T1_Related_Legislative_and_Regulatory_Developments.html)

3 Capco Smart Suite is a modular, AI-driven platform designed to transform capital markets operations, enhance compliance, and optimize client servicing through intelligent automation and data-driven insights. https://www.capco.com/industries/capital-markets/capital-markets-smart-suite 

    

  

          

Contact us

title: Fund lifecycle management: integrated FLCM Control Tower for asset managers
snippet: Fund lifecycle management is increasingly becoming a strategic control tower capability for asset managers. Firms that modernize and optimize this capability will reduce operational risk, accelerate...
fullText:
Fund lifecycle management is increasingly becoming a strategic control tower capability for asset managers. Firms that modernize and optimize this capability will reduce operational risk, accelerate time-to-market, improve product governance and create a more scalable foundation for growth, distribution, regulatory reporting and handling of fund lifecycle events. 
          

This papers examines:

    

Fund management complexity and design faults

    

Why lifecycle velocity with control is becoming a management priority

    

What good looks like in a fund lifecycle control tower

    

Where value is created and how data is governed

    

Key benefits of a fund lifecycle management control tower

    

Enabling architecture

    

Our recommended approach.

The challenge: hidden complexity behind every fund

From the outside, a fund is designed to look simple. It has a name, a strategy, a prospectus and a place in a product range. For investors and distributors, this simplicity is essential. It allows the product to be understood, compared, assessed and eventually selected.

Inside an asset manager, the same fund is one of the most complex operating objects the firm manages. Every lifecycle event creates a trail of decisions, data, documents, approvals, controls and external dependencies. When the fund lifecycle is not governed end-to-end, complexity becomes a constraint on growth, control and scalability.

The next performance frontier is fund lifecycle velocity with control: the ability to launch, change, govern, report on, distribute and close funds faster, without weakening accountability. For asset managers, this is no longer a narrow operational improvement topic. It is becoming a critical execution capability.

Asset managers have industrialized investment processes, distribution channels and reporting outputs. Many have not yet industrialized the fund lifecycle management process itself. That gap is now becoming visible in delayed launches, duplicated operational effort, inconsistent product data, weak management visibility and slower adoption of controlled automation.

This rticle is not about investment management. It is not about how portfolios are built or how performance is generated. It is about the operating capability around the fund as a product that needs to be managed and maintained from end to end: how it is created, approved, launched, maintained, changed, reported on, distributed and closed.

That distinction matters: the administrative and governance-heavy work around funds is often less visible than investment management, but it is critical to growth, control, client experience and regulatory resilience. A fund range cannot scale if every launch, change or reporting cycle is handled as an ad-hoc project and depends on fragmented coordination and individual memory.

The speed at which AI is being adopted throughout organizations reinforces this point: the more lifecycle information becomes digital and traceable, the more it can support AI-enabled document intelligence, exception detection, workflow assistance and decision support. But AI is an enabler, the strategic question is whether asset managers have the lifecycle operating model, data foundation and governance to use it safely and effectively.

Controlled AI adoption means using AI inside governed workflows, on approved data sources, with clear ownership, traceable outputs, human review and documented controls. Without these foundations, AI may improve local productivity but will struggle to create reliable enterprise value.

The strategic question is therefore not whether individual fund lifecycle activities can be digitized. It is whether asset managers can establish the missing operating layer around the fund: a lifecycle control tower that connects decisions, data, workflows, controls, documents and third-party dependencies across the full product journey. This is the capability required to support growth and resilience and enable AI adoption within a governed operating model.

The problem: lifecycle work is fragmented by design

Most asset managers have historically optimized around investment management, performance generation and distribution growth. That is understandable, as these are the areas most directly linked to growth, revenue and market positioning. Fund lifecycle management has often remained the administrative layer around the product; the result is not simply inefficient processes, it is structural fragmentation.

Fund lifecycle management work is spread across product teams, legal, compliance, operations, reporting, finance, risk, distribution, fund administrators, custodians and other service providers. Each function owns a legitimate part of the process, but the end-to-end lifecycle is often not owned, orchestrated or governed as one capability.

The typical operating model reflects this history: fund launches and product changes may be tracked in spreadsheets; approvals may sit in email chains; documents may be stored across shared folders, document repositories, and local drives; product data may be duplicated in a mix of internal and external static-data tools; controls may exist, but they are often embedded locally rather than connected across the lifecycle.

The practical consequences are familiar. The same product data is entered multiple times. Data points do not always match across systems. Teams spend time reconciling what should already be consistent. Approvals are slow because ownership is unclear. Evidence is collected late, often when audit, compliance, or reporting teams request it. Key individuals become the real operating model because they know where information sits and which handoffs matter.

The impact is practical. A fee change may be updated in one static-data tool but not reflected consistently in factsheets, distributor feeds, regulatory templates and internal reporting. A new share class may be approved commercially but delayed operationally because document production, provider setup, data creation and market registration are not managed through one lifecycle view. A board or audit request may trigger manual reconstruction because decision history and evidence were not captured as work was performed.

Many firms have digitized individual steps. They have workflow tools, data warehouses, reporting platforms, document systems and service provider portals. Yet the fund lifecycle itself remains poorly orchestrated. The industry has digitized many components of fund operations, but it has not established the operating layer that connects them across the fund lifecycle as a whole.

This is the missing role of the fund lifecycle control tower: to connect functional ownership, workflow execution, governed product data, documents, controls, evidence and external dependencies into one coordinated capability. Without this layer, firms may continue to improve individual tools while leaving the underlying fragmentation intact.

The same limitation constrains AI readiness. AI cannot reliably summarize, recommend or support execution across a lifecycle with weak data ownership, inconsistent evidence and fragmented process metadata. In that environment, AI may accelerate inconsistency rather than solve it.

Why now: fund lifecycle management is moving from back-office process to strategic capability

Fund lifecycle management can no longer be treated as administrative plumbing. The cost of fragmentation is now visible at executive level: delayed launches, slower product changes, inconsistent regulatory evidence, duplicated cost, weak management visibility and constrained AI adoption.

What used to be a coordination problem is becoming a strategic execution problem. The pressure is coming from four directions: growth, control, cost and AI readiness.

    

Growth Firms need to launch, adapt, register, and distribute products faster, while managing more domiciles, wrappers, share classes, ESG variations, and white-label structures. A slow lifecycle model directly limits commercial responsiveness.

    

Control Disclosures, regulatory templates, investor communications, and governance processes all depend on accurate, consistent, and traceable product data. When lifecycle data is fragmented, reporting becomes remediation and control becomes dependent on manual reconstruction.

    

Cost Teams spend too much time rekeying data, reconciling inconsistencies, chasing approvals, and reconstructing evidence after the fact. The cost is often hidden because it is absorbed across functions, but it is material.

    

AI readiness AI-enabled productivity will not scale safely unless it is connected to governed workflows, trusted data, controls, and clear ownership. Without those foundations, AI remains a set of isolated productivity experiments rather than an enterprise capability.

Senior management expectations are also changing. Executives do not only want to know whether a fund was launched. They want to know where each lifecycle event stands, what is outstanding, where risk is building, and which decisions have already been made.

AI and automation create further pressure. Many firms are experimenting with AI to improve productivity, but isolated experimentation will not create enterprise value unless it is connected to governed workflows, trusted data, controls and clear operating model ownership.

This is why lifecycle velocity with control is becoming a management priority: firms need to move faster across launches, changes, registrations, reporting cycles and lifecycle events, without reducing governance discipline. As product ranges become more complex, lifecycle fragmentation no longer creates only operational inefficiency. It increasingly compresses operating margins and determines how quickly the firm can convert product strategy into revenue.

What good looks like: the fund lifecycle control tower

Modern fund lifecycle management requires a control tower. This is not a monolithic system and not a dashboard on top of fragmented processes. It is the operating layer that connects product decisions, lifecycle data, workflow execution, document production, control evidence and third-party dependencies across the full product journey.

Its purpose is not only to show what is happening. It is to make fund lifecycle management execution repeatable, auditable and scalable. It should help the firm answer practical questions quickly:

    

What is the status of this launch or change?

    

Which approvals are outstanding?

    

Which product data is missing or inconsistent?

    

Which documents need to be updated?

    

Who owns the next action?

    

What evidence exists for audit, compliance, board review or management oversight?

In Capco’s view, the FLCM Control Tower is not primarily a technology construct. It is a domain-led operating-model and data capability, enabled by technology. Its effectiveness depends on five connected capabilities that together provide the framework for lifecycle modernization:

    

Workflow orchestration Lifecycle activities need clear steps, owners, handoffs, service levels, approvals, escalations and exception paths. This does not remove local expertise. It makes it visible and repeatable.

    

A single source of product truth Fund lifecycle execution depends on product data that is consistent, reusable and governed. The control tower should not create another data silo, it should connect to golden sources and expose trusted lifecycle data to the teams, systems, reports and documents that need it.

    

Embedded controls and auditability Controls should sit inside the lifecycle rather than after it. Evidence should be captured as work is performed. Approval history, decision rationale, document and data versions and exceptions should be traceable by design.

    

Integrated document and report production Fund documents and reports should reuse governed product data wherever possible. Prospectuses, key information documents (KIDs), factsheets, regulatory templates, distributor packs and committee papers should not be recreated from disconnected sources.

    

Open integration with the asset management ecosystem Fund lifecycle management depends on a multitude of external partners and stakeholders (fund administrators, custodians, transfer agents, data providers, reporting vendors, regulators and distributors). The FLCM Control Tower must connect internal teams with external dependencies in a controlled way.

In practice, this means that a proposed product change should show the impacted share classes, documents, reports, distributor feeds, service provider actions, approvals, evidence requirements and target completion dates in one controlled workflow.

AI can strengthen this model when it is embedded into the governed lifecycle. Relevant use cases include launch-status summarization, document comparison, missing-data detection, exception analytics, draft committee materials and workflow assistance.

At a more advanced level of maturity, selected fund lifecycle processes could be supported through controlled agentic execution. In this model, a user interacts with an AI agent that can analyze documents, assemble information, invoke approved deterministic tools and coordinate next actions within defined workflow stages, policy rules, approval gates and escalation paths. The agent provides flexibility in handling the circumstances of an individual lifecycle case, while the process boundaries and control requirements remain fixed.

These capabilities should support accountable teams; they should not replace product approval, regulatory sign-off, data ownership, risk acceptance or other material judgement. This principle also applies to controlled agentic execution: an agent may prepare a case, coordinate permitted actions and recommend the next step, but defined decisions and exceptions must remain with product, legal, compliance, risk, data and governance owners. This boundary is essential if AI is to improve speed and consistency without weakening control.

The FLCM Control Tower is therefore not a technology slogan or an additional application. It is the operating model through which asset managers create lifecycle transparency, embed control, coordinate execution and scale product complexity. The following sections examine where this model creates value and the data, technology and governance foundations required to make it work.

The lifecycle lens: where value is created

The lifecycle lens matters because value is created across the full product journey, not only at launch. A modern lifecycle capability should improve decision quality, market readiness, change execution, reporting reliability and closure discipline.

Value is not created by optimizing one step in isolation. It is created by managing the fund lifecycle as an end-to-end chain of decisions, data, documents, approvals, controls and external dependencies. The opportunity is to improve how the firm moves from product idea to market launch, from launch to ongoing change, from change to reporting and eventually from reporting to closure.

The lifecycle perspective shows where fragmentation creates delay, risk, rework and weak visibility – and where a more governed lifecycle capability can create value.

    

Ideation and product development: Firms need to capture the commercial rationale, target investors, investment strategy, share-class needs, distribution ambition and feasibility constraints. A stronger lifecycle model creates structured business cases and decision records. AI can support this stage by summarizing market inputs, comparing proposals with the existing product range, identifying potential overlaps and drafting committee materials. Final decisions should remain with accountable product and investment governance bodies.

    

Registration and setup: The operating model must coordinate application packs, regulatory submissions, launch readiness checks and operational dependencies. This is where fragmentation is often most visible. AI can assist by checking completeness, comparing submitted documents against approved product data and identifying missing or inconsistent information.

    

Distribution and publication:The challenge shifts to market readiness. The firm must manage distributor onboarding, market registrations, data dissemination and document publication. The right data and documents must reach the right markets, channels and investor segments. AI can help identify market-specific documentation gaps and summarize distribution readiness by jurisdiction.

    

Ongoing product management: Lifecycle work becomes continuous: static data changes, fee updates, structural changes, board approvals, mergers, restructurings and share-class rationalization all need controlled execution. A lifecycle control tower can show which systems, reports, distribution channels and provider obligations are impacted by a proposed change.

    

Reporting: Reporting is another area where fund lifecycle modernization creates visible value. Regulatory, client, management, tax and template-based reporting should reuse governed lifecycle data rather than recreate and reconcile it each time. AI can support reporting narratives, variance explanations and anomaly detection, but sign-off must remain controlled.

    

Liquidation and closure: These activities should be treated as a lifecycle process, not an ad hoc project. The firm must manage investor and regulator communications, final NAV and accounting activity, provider termination, final reporting, document retention and evidence packs. AI can help generate closure checklists and identify outstanding obligations, but the process still needs clear ownership and controls.

The data foundation: the FLCM Control Tower depends on a governed fund lifecycle data model

The FLCM Control Tower cannot operate effectively without a governed fund lifecycle data model. Workflow visibility alone is not enough if the underlying product data remains duplicated, inconsistent, weakly owned or disconnected from documents, reporting obligations and lifecycle events.

This is where many transformation efforts under-deliver: they digitize tasks but leave the underlying data model unchanged. The result is faster movement of inconsistent data across more screens. That is not lifecycle transformation; it is the automation of fragmentation.

Product data is broader than traditional static data. It includes the fund hierarchy, legal structure, domicile, share classes, fees, investment restrictions, service providers, distribution permissions, documentation status, regulatory obligations, lifecycle events, reporting dependencies and closure evidence. It also includes commercial and governance context, such as product rationale, decision records, review outcomes and change history.

For example, a lifecycle data model should not only store the fund name, domicile, ISIN and share-class attributes. It should also connect those data points to approval status, document versions, distribution permissions, reporting dependencies, service-provider obligations and change history.

The data model must support operational execution, regulatory reporting, product governance, document generation, management information, analytics and AI-enabled assistance. It must also handle variation across domiciles and operating structures. Cross-border asset managers need data models that can support Switzerland, Luxembourg, Ireland and other fund hubs without redesigning the lifecycle for each location.

This matters especially for AI: document comparison requires trusted reference data; summarization requires reliable source documents and version control; exception detection requires complete and consistent historical records; workflow recommendations require process metadata, ownership, and business rules; reporting assistance requires lineage, approved calculations and clear sign-off points.

AI does not fix weak data foundations but rather exposes and amplifies them. If product data is incomplete, duplicated, inconsistent or poorly owned, AI will not remove the problem, it will rather scale it.

Historization, lineage, reconciliation, validation and access control are therefore not technical extras, they are core business requirements. The target state is not one big database. It is a governed, reusable, traceable lifecycle data layer that can be consumed by workflows, documents, reports, analytics and controlled automation.

The enabling architecture: a composable FLCM Control Tower, not a monolithic platform

The FLCM Control Tower does not require another monolithic platform. It requires a connected lifecycle architecture that orchestrates the systems and capabilities asset managers already have. Most firms operate portfolio platforms, reporting tools, document repositories, data warehouses, administrator feeds, custodian interfaces, risk systems, regulatory reporting engines and distribution platforms. The challenge is usually not the absence of technology. It is the absence of an operating and integration layer that connects these components across the lifecycle.

The technology architecture supporting the FLCM Control Tower should therefore be composable, not monolithic. It should connect existing capabilities where they are fit for purpose and standardize the lifecycle layer where the firm needs consistency, transparency and control.

The architecture should support modular services, open APIs, workflow engines, reporting integration, role-based access control, audit monitoring and third-party connectivity. It should be flexible enough to support different combinations of domiciles, asset classes, fund wrappers, service provider models and management company structures.

In Capco’s view, technology choices should follow the operating model and data choices, not the other way around. The firm first needs to define which fund lifecycle capabilities should be common, where local variation is justified, which data should be governed centrally, and which controls must be embedded into the workflow. Technology should then enable that model through integration, automation and management visibility.

AI-enabled components should be added selectively, where there is clear value creation and a controlled operating model. The use cases should also be sequenced by maturity.

    

Assistive intelligence is the natural starting point: document classification, extraction, comparison, summarization, retrieval across governed product data and policies and AI-assisted drafting for committee papers, change summaries, regulatory packs and reporting commentary.

    

Exception intelligence comes next: missing-data detection, anomaly detection, readiness-gap identification and exception analytics across lifecycle events, documents, reports and provider dependencies.

    

Controlled agentic execution is the more advanced stage: for suitable lifecycle processes, a user can interact with an AI agent to progress a specific case. The agent can analyze documents, assemble information, invoke approved tools, coordinate tasks, propose next actions and evaluate whether defined completion criteria have been met.

The agentic loop combines different types of capabilities. AI components can support activities such as document analysis, drafting, synthesis and interaction. Deterministic tools should perform calculations, rule-based checks, validations and other activities where precision and reproducibility are required. The agent then uses the resulting information to progress the case, repeat an activity, request input or escalate an exception.

This should not be interpreted as autonomous lifecycle management. Controlled agentic execution operates inside predefined workflow stages, permissions, policy rules, approval gates and escalation paths. Product approval, regulatory sign-off, risk acceptance and other material decisions remain with accountable human owners.

These capabilities should sit inside the governed lifecycle architecture, not outside it as uncontrolled productivity tools. For controlled agentic execution, the firm must define which data, systems and tools the agent may access; which actions it may perform; which completion criteria it may evaluate; and where it must stop, request approval or escalate.

Human approval gates, evidence capture, action logs, control checks, monitoring and fallback procedures are non-negotiable when lifecycle activities are automated or AI-assisted. The architecture must also allow the firm to reconstruct what information the agent used, which tools it invoked, what outputs were produced and which human decisions were taken.

Controlled agentic execution should therefore be treated as a credible advanced destination for selected processes, not as the starting point for lifecycle modernization. Its effectiveness depends on the workflow, data, integration, control and evidence foundations established in the earlier stages of maturity.

Firms should avoid big-bang replacement where possible. Existing systems should be retained where they work. New capabilities should be introduced around clear value pools, such as fund launches, static data changes, regulatory document production, reporting readiness or lifecycle events.

The implication is simple: the lifecycle control tower should be enabled through a connected, composable architecture, not delivered as another isolated application.

Benefits: what executives should care about

The business case is fund lifecycle velocity with control: the ability to move faster across product launches, changes, registrations, reporting cycles and closures, while reducing the manual effort, evidence gaps and coordination risk that usually come with scale. For executives, the value is not only process efficiency, it is improved management of product complexity.

The FLCM Control Tower improves four outcomes that matter directly to executives: speed, cost, control and scalability. These are not separate benefits delivered by isolated initiatives. They result from the same underlying operating capability: fund lifecycle work becomes visible, product data becomes reusable, controls are embedded into execution, and cross-functional and third-party dependencies become actively manageable.

    

Faster product moves: A governed fund lifecycle model reduces the time lost between commercial decision and operational readiness. Launches, new share classes, fee changes, market registrations, document updates and lifecycle events can move through predefined steps, with clearer ownership and fewer late-stage surprises. Executives gain better visibility of where delays are building, which dependencies are blocking progress, and where intervention is required.

    

Lower hidden cost: Much of the cost of lifecycle fragmentation is absorbed across functions rather than visible in one budget line. Product, legal, compliance, operations, reporting, distribution and provider teams spend time re-keying data, reconciling inconsistencies, chasing approvals and reconstructing evidence. A stronger lifecycle model reduces this hidden effort by reusing governed data, standardizing repeatable workflows, and capturing evidence as work is performed.

    

Stronger control: Lifecycle control improves when approvals, decision history, data changes, document versions, exceptions and evidence are embedded into the workflow rather than collected after the fact. This strengthens audit readiness, regulatory confidence, board reporting and management oversight. It also reduces reliance on individual knowledge, because the operating model no longer depends on a small number of people knowing where information sits and which handoffs matter.

    

Scalable growth: Growth becomes harder to manage when every new fund, domicile, share class, distribution arrangement or lifecycle event adds another layer of manual coordination. A governed lifecycle capability creates reusable patterns across products, jurisdictions, providers, documents, reports and controls. This allows firms to scale complexity more deliberately, without adding proportional headcount or creating new local workarounds for every market or product variation.

The same control-tower capability also creates the foundation for controlled AI adoption. AI-enabled document comparison, exception detection, reporting support and workflow assistance are more useful when they operate on trusted data, clear ownership, documented decisions and traceable evidence. This turns AI from a set of local productivity experiments into a capability that can support lifecycle execution at enterprise level.

Management should be able to track the health of the fund lifecycle through practical indicators: cycle times, open bottlenecks, data-quality exceptions, evidence completeness, document readiness, provider dependencies and status by fund, domicile, lifecycle event or reporting cycle. This is where lifecycle modernization becomes an executive management capability, not only an operational improvement.

Capco’s recommended approach

Capco’s view is that the winners will not be the firms that simply digitize more fund lifecycle tasks. They will be the firms that establish a true fund lifecycle control tower: a governed, data-led operating capability that connects execution across the product journey and embeds AI selectively as the underlying workflow, data and control foundations mature.

Capco helps asset managers move from fragmented fund lifecycle activity to a controlled, AI-ready lifecycle capability through seven practical moves. The sequence matters: the work starts with understanding where fragmentation creates value leakage, then builds the operating model, data foundation, governance and integration layer required to scale.

1.	Diagnose lifecycle fragmentation

The starting point is to map how lifecycle work actually happens today: where decisions are made, where data is created, where documents are produced, where controls sit, and where evidence is captured. The objective is not to document processes for their own sake. It is to identify where fragmentation creates delay, risk, rework, data-quality issues or reliance on individual knowledge.

2.	Define the target lifecycle capability model

Firms need to be clear about which fund lifecycle capabilities should be standardized and where variation is required by domicile, asset class, product type or operating structure. This is where the lifecycle control tower should be defined in practical terms: which capabilities it owns, which activities it orchestrates, how it interacts with functional teams and providers, and how it gives management a reliable view of lifecycle status, risk and performance.

3.	Build the product and lifecycle data foundation

Fund lifecycle management modernization depends on trusted product data. Asset managers need to clarify ownership, golden sources, data standards, lineage, history, access rights and reuse across workflows, documents, reports and controls. This foundation is also what determines whether AI can be used safely for document intelligence, exception detection, reporting support and workflow assistance. For controlled agentic execution, governance must extend to the actions the agent is permitted to perform. These boundaries should be embedded into the workflow and evidenced as the case progresses.

4.	Prioritize workflow use cases

The best starting point is usually not the full fund lifecycle at once. Firms should select high-friction journeys where better orchestration can create visible impact, such as fund launches, static-data changes, regulatory document production, distributor onboarding, fund events or reporting readiness. Each use case should be designed with clear roles, controls, data inputs, approval gates and evidence requirements.

5.	Modernize through integration, not replacement alone

Most asset managers already have many of the required technology components. The challenge is to connect them into a coherent fund lifecycle architecture. Existing platforms should be retained where they work, while new capabilities should be introduced where the firm needs better workflow orchestration, data reuse, document production, reporting integration or controlled AI enablement.

6.	Embed governance into the operating model

Fund lifecycle management modernization only works if accountability is explicit. Roles, decision rights, service levels, exception paths, control points and evidence requirements need to be built into the way work is performed. The same principle applies to AI-enabled use cases: they require clear ownership, approved data boundaries, testing, monitoring, documentation and human oversight.

Capco helps firms separate AI use cases that can be scaled safely from those that should remain experimental until data quality, evidence, controls and ownership are stronger. This is where domain expertise matters: the value of AI depends not only on the model or tool, but on whether the lifecycle process around it is controlled enough to absorb it.

7.	Scale iteratively through reusable building blocks

Finally, asset managers should start with a small number of priority use cases, prove value, and then extend across products, jurisdictions, asset classes and lifecycle stages. Each release should create assets that can be reused: process patterns, data models, control libraries, workflow components, reporting templates, integration capabilities and approved tool services.

Controlled agentic execution should be treated as an advanced destination for suitable lifecycle processes. It should be introduced once the relevant workflow stages, data inputs, decision rights, controls, evidence requirements, integrations and escalation paths have been established and proven. Firms should not place an agent on top of a fragmented process and expect it to compensate for the absence of an operating model.

For asset managers, the priority is not to add another tool to an already fragmented landscape. It is to build the operating model, data foundation, governance and integration layer that make lifecycle execution faster, safer and more scalable.

This is where Capco is positioned to help: combining asset management domain knowledge with operating-model, data, AI, technology and delivery expertise to design and implement the lifecycle control tower and progressively enable more advanced forms of controlled automation.

The objective is not simply to improve individual workflows. It is to help firms establish the operating layer that connects product decisions, governed data, controls, documents, reporting and third-party dependencies across a repeatable and scalable lifecycle model.

The opportunity is not simply to make fund lifecycle management work more efficient, it is to turn fund lifecycle management into a platform for product growth, regulatory resilience and controlled automation.

For UK and EU insurers, having the right policies and frameworks in place is no longer enough. As supervisory scrutiny intensifies, firms must demonstrate that their governance, data and controls deliver the intended outcomes.
          

      

With 2027 approaching, five areas demand particular attention:

    

Operational resilience: Strengthening cyber resilience and third-party oversight

    

Financial crime: Establishing consistent controls supported by reliable data

    

Financial risk: Demonstrating capital and liquidity resilience under stress

    

Finance: Preparing financial reporting for IFRS 18

    

Non-financial risk: Delivering clear customer disclosures and demonstrating effective outcomes

Drawing on our experience supporting major insurance groups, we examine these priorities and share practical lessons on strengthening accountability, connecting data and controls, and embedding regulatory compliance into everyday operations.
